cards.title: The Internet's Broken: Why 'Local-First' Privacy Tools Are Blowing Up Right Now
cards.thesis: People are fed up with the internet constantly demanding personal data, showing intrusive ads, and making basic tasks like logging in or solving CAPTCHAs a nightmare. This frustration, combined with a growing desire for privacy and local-first (meaning, runs on your device, not in the cloud) tools, creates a massive opportunity for builders to create apps that make the web feel usable and safe again without sending your data anywhere.

evidence.text: Users are reporting that the internet feels 'no longer accessible' due to 'tons of CAPTCHAs' that are 'impossible to solve,' constant demands for '2FA' (two-factor authentication, a security check) that often fail, websites blocking copy-paste, and intrusive requests for microphone access.

A new open-source project called 'Yap' offers on-device voice dictation for macOS, where 'everything runs locally and never leaves your computer.' This showcases the appeal of tools that prioritize local processing and privacy.

Builders are increasingly worried about the 'security implications of running/installing projects' from places like GitHub, noting it's 'so easy to inject back doors and malware into software projects now a days,' making them hesitant to try new tools.
Even major AI services like Claude AI are experiencing outages for over a week with no support, highlighting the unreliability of relying solely on external cloud providers.
There's growing concern about pervasive advertising, with examples like BMWs showing 'in-car ads for Spiderman' as a 'surprise alert,' contributing to a feeling of digital intrusion.

cards.opportunity: Everyone's complaining that the internet is broken with CAPTCHAs, constant data demands, and intrusive ads, making it feel 'no longer accessible.' But nobody's really built a local-first, privacy-preserving 'digital assistant' that proactively helps you navigate these daily annoyances without sending your data to the cloud. Imagine an app that lives in your menu bar, like Yap, that can intelligently manage temporary identities for one-off sign-ups, or even just make copy-pasting work everywhere without asking for mic access. The first person to ship a tool that genuinely makes the internet feel less hostile, by keeping everything local, will own this frustrated-user market.

cards.title: Forget GPT-4: Small, Cheap AI Models Are Secretly Crushing It on Niche Tasks
cards.thesis: Builders are discovering that you don't always need the biggest, most expensive AI models. Smaller, open-source AI models (which are freely available to use and modify) are proving surprisingly effective and pleasant to work with. For specific jobs, a little targeted training on these affordable models can make them outperform the 'frontier' models that cost a fortune.

evidence.text: People are finding that using open (freely available) AI models feels really good, suggesting they are getting surprisingly strong results.

Someone showed that for just $500 in training costs, a smaller 9-billion-parameter open-source AI model (a 'parameter' is a measure of an AI's size and complexity) could beat the top, cutting-edge AI models at reviewing product catalogs.

cards.opportunity: Everyone's still defaulting to paying top dollar for generalist AI models like GPT-4 to handle all sorts of tasks. But these signals show that a small, targeted investment in fine-tuning an open model can achieve superior results for niche problems like 'catalog review' at a fraction of the cost. You could launch a hyper-specialized AI agent for a specific, data-heavy industry problem—think 'automated compliance checks for financial documents' or 'sentiment analysis for medical reviews'—and blow away the competition on both price and accuracy by leveraging these cheap, powerful, fine-tuned open models.
